buses.name: CubeSat 12U Bus
buses.description: A shoebox-size satellite body. Tiny and cheap, fits one small instrument.

buses.name: Small Bus
buses.description: A washing-machine-size body for focused missions with up to two instruments.

buses.name: Medium Bus
buses.description: A car-size body with room for four instruments. Carries a spare reaction wheel.

buses.name: Large Bus
buses.description: A bus-size body for flagship missions with six instruments. Carries a spare reaction wheel.

solarArrays.name: Silicon Solar Array
solarArrays.description: Proven silicon cells. Cheap, but heavier and they lose 3% of their power every year.

solarArrays.name: Triple-Junction GaAs Array
solarArrays.description: High-efficiency multi-layer cells: more than twice the power per kilogram, slower aging, double the price.

rtg.name: Radioisotope Power Unit
rtg.description: Makes electricity from the heat of decaying plutonium. Works in darkness and dust, far from the Sun. Very expensive.

batteries.name: Li-ion Battery
batteries.description: Standard rechargeable battery. Use at most 40% of its charge each eclipse to make it last for years.

batteries.name: High-Energy Li-ion Battery
batteries.description: Lighter high-energy cells that tolerate deeper discharge (50%).

computers.name: Standard Flight Computer
computers.description: A reliable flight computer with 64 GB of storage.

computers.name: Rad-Hard Computer with Compression
computers.description: Radiation-hardened, handles emergencies on its own, compresses data to half its size, 512 GB of storage.

adcs.name: Magnetorquers + Sun Sensors
adcs.description: Electromagnets push against Earth's magnetic field. Light and cheap, but only roughly accurate (±5°) and useless far from Earth.

adcs.name: Reaction Wheels + Star Tracker
adcs.description: Spinning wheels turn the spacecraft; a star camera tells it where it points. Accurate to ±0.05°.

adcs.name: Precision Pointing System
adcs.description: Fine-guidance sensors and ultra-smooth wheels for telescopes: ±0.001°.

propulsion.name: No Propulsion
propulsion.description: No engine. Light and simple — but you cannot change your orbit, avoid debris or deorbit.

propulsion.name: Cold-Gas Thrusters
propulsion.description: Puffs of compressed gas. Simple and safe but weak (Isp 65 s); holds at most 20 kg of gas.

propulsion.name: Hydrazine Monopropellant
propulsion.description: Hydrazine thrusters (Isp 220 s). The classic choice for keeping a satellite in its orbit.

propulsion.name: Bipropellant Engine
propulsion.description: Fuel and oxidizer burn together (Isp 315 s). Strong enough for big orbit changes like reaching GEO or Mars orbit.

propulsion.name: Electric Hall Thrusters
propulsion.description: Ion-like thrusters use electricity to push gas out very fast (Isp 1600 s): tiny propellant mass, but weak thrust — reaching orbit takes months and needs 1,000 W of power.

radios.name: UHF Radio
radios.description: A simple amateur-style radio. Very slow (9.6 kbps) and only works close to Earth.

radios.name: S-Band Transmitter
radios.description: A dependable radio for commands and modest data rates.

radios.name: X-Band Transmitter
radios.description: The standard science downlink: fast, works from Earth orbit to Mars.

radios.name: Ka-Band Transmitter
radios.description: Very high data rates, but heavy rain at the ground station can interrupt the signal.

hga.name: High-Gain Dish Antenna (1.5 m)
hga.description: A 1.5 m dish focuses the radio beam 20× more strongly. It must be aimed precisely (needs reaction wheels).

groundNetworks.name: University Ground Station (Cairo, 3 m dish)
groundNetworks.description: One small dish. Cheap, few minutes per pass, cannot reach beyond Earth orbit.

groundNetworks.name: Commercial Polar Network (several 5–7 m dishes)
groundNetworks.description: Stations near the poles see polar orbits on almost every pass.

groundNetworks.name: Deep-Space Network (34–70 m dishes on 3 continents)
groundNetworks.description: Huge dishes that can hear spacecraft at the Moon, L2 and Mars. Time is shared, so you get scheduled hours.
